title: Calendaring and scheduling website
description: Let people register, create events, invite others by email, and view registered invitees' free/busy information. Explain the overlap SQL and how the database scales beyond one machine.
focus: relational modeling, internal/external attendees, recurring events, time zones, free/busy correctness, and partitioning.

children.value: A product design with a schema and a query at its heart
Design a calendaring and scheduling site.

People register, create events, invite others by email, and — for registered invitees — see free/busy before they schedule. The interesting parts are the relational schema, the overlap query, and what breaks when the data outgrows one database.
Structured from the supplied prompt, interviewer tips, and scoring rubric. This is one defensible design; capacity numbers and product choices are labeled as illustrative.

Model users, events, attendees, and pre-expanded busy blocks in a relational database. Free/busy is a half-open interval-overlap query. Sharding by user_id makes per-user calendars and free/busy local, at the cost of fanning out an event's busy blocks to each attendee's shard and reasoning about the resulting eventual consistency.
The two follow-ups — the overlap SQL and the partitioning strategy — are the highest-signal deliverables. Lead with requirements and a schema, then earn each of them.

A website where people register accounts and manage a personal calendar of events. An organizer can invite others by email address. If an invited email belongs to a registered user, the organizer can see that invitee's free/busy so they can pick a time that works.
Register/login; create, view, edit, delete events; invite people by email; RSVP; and view free/busy for registered invitees over a time range.
The SQL query that decides whether a group of users is free during a time block.
How to partition the data past one database, and the issues that follow.
The interviewer tips ask for coverage of
the website, the system architecture, each component, and the DB schema
— plus partitioning, caching, and the consistency issues they create. So this answer keeps the schema and query central rather than treating them as an afterthought.
How this differs from a pure infra problem
Scale matters, but the discriminating signal here is
a correct data model and a correct overlap query
, then a sharding plan whose consistency trade-offs you can articulate. A vague box diagram with no schema or query will not clear the bar.
register with email + password; log in; each user has a calendar and a home time zone.
create/read/update/delete events with a title, start/end, time zone, optional recurrence, and a busy/free marker.
invite people by email; registered invitees get an in-app invite, unregistered ones get an email to join; invitees RSVP (accept / decline / tentative).
for a set of registered invitees over a time range, return when each is busy so the organizer can schedule.
Recurrence makes free/busy hard: a rule can imply thousands of occurrences that are not rows.
Yes. Store an iCalendar-style rule plus exceptions; expand within a bounded window.
Privacy: busy intervals only, not titles/details, unless shared.
Busy/tentative/free blocks only; no event content across users by default.
How do time zones and all-day events behave?
DST and floating all-day events are classic correctness traps.
Store absolute UTC instants plus the original zone and rule; all-day events are date-based.
Cross-user reads can lag; your own edits should not.
Read-your-writes for your own calendar; free/busy of others may be seconds-stale.
Decides single-DB vs sharded, and drives follow-up 2.
Order of 100M users; reads far exceed writes.
Rooms/resources, external calendar sync, notifications channel?
Common extensions that can balloon scope.
Email notifications in scope; rooms/sync/push are labeled extensions.
Events are user data; never lose an accepted meeting. Replicated primary storage plus backups.
Strong for a user's own writes/RSVP; free/busy across users may be eventually consistent within seconds. No double-booking silently hidden.
Interactive scheduling: free/busy for a handful of invitees over a week in well under ~200ms.
Reading your calendar and sending invites should tolerate a replica or worker failure.
Grows past one database (follow-up 2): partition by user and keep per-user reads local.
Authn/authz; free/busy and event details gated by sharing rules; invitee emails not leaked.
Times are stored as absolute UTC instants. Intervals are half-open
so back-to-back meetings do not conflict. Declined and cancelled events are not busy. Recurrence must be expanded before it can be range-queried. Free/busy reveals availability, not content.
Requirements and a sketch first, details second
The rubric rewards clarifying requirements and sketching a high-level design before diving in, then anticipating issues rather than waiting for hints. Use the progression:
working behavior → visible limitation → alternatives → justified change
Illustrative 45-minute plan; adjust to the round.
Four functional pillars, privacy of free/busy, time-zone/recurrence flags, scale.
Why it eventually exceeds one DB (justifies follow-up 2).
User, Event, Attendee, BusyBlock; the create-event and free/busy endpoints.
Web/app/DB/cache/queue sketch, then the actual tables and indexes.
The overlap SQL (with recurrence caveat) and sharding-by-user with consistency issues.
Caching, failures, and the trade-offs you chose.

Meet all axes and exceed at least two (depth or fault tolerance). Strong signals: raising recurrence, time zones, and free/busy privacy unprompted; writing a correct half-open overlap query; and choosing a shard key whose consistency cost you name and mitigate.
Event writes = 100M × 5 / 604,800 s ≈ 827 events/second average (higher at business-hours peaks)
Reads (calendar views + free/busy), ~30× writes ≈ 25,000 reads/second average
Events retained = 100M × 5 × 52 × 3 = 78 billion rows ≈ 23.4 TB at ~300 bytes
Attendee rows = 78B × 4 = 312 billion ≈ 25 TB at ~80 bytes
Busy blocks (accepted/tentative, plus expanded recurrences) are of similar order

tens of terabytes of hot relational data plus indexes, replicas, and busy-block materialization comfortably exceeds one database node. That is exactly why follow-up 2 (partitioning) is on the table. Writes are modest; the pressure is data volume and per-user read latency, not raw QPS.
These are transparent order-of-magnitude figures, not a product benchmark. The point is the conclusion, not the third significant figure.
Name the nouns before the tables
A registered account: email (unique), credentials, display name, home time zone.
A container of events owned by a user. One default per user; modeling it separately allows multiple/shared calendars later.
A meeting/appointment: organizer, title, start/end instant, time zone, optional recurrence rule, busy/free marker, status.
A link between an event and an invitee (by user_id if registered, else by email), plus RSVP status and role.
A derived, pre-expanded busy interval for one user — the read-optimized form that makes free/busy a simple range scan and shards cleanly.
An outbound message (invite, RSVP update, reminder) produced asynchronously.
Actors overlap: the organizer is a user; every attendee who is registered is also a user with their own calendar. That overlap is the crux of both the schema and the sharding discussion.
REST is the right default here
The current user is derived from the session/token, never from the request body.

POST /v1/users                 register {email, password, name, timezone}
POST /v1/sessions              login -> session cookie / token

POST /v1/events                create an event
  { title, start, end, timezone, all_day,
    recurrence_rule, transparency: "opaque"|"transparent",
    attendee_emails: [ ... ] }
GET  /v1/events?from=&to=      calendar view for the current user
PATCH  /v1/events/{id}         edit (a time change triggers busy-block fan-out)
DELETE /v1/events/{id}         cancel

POST /v1/events/{id}/rsvp      { status: "accepted"|"declined"|"tentative" }

POST /v1/free-busy            availability for a scheduling grid
  { emails: [ ... ], from, to }
  -> per email: registered? and [ {start, end, status} ] busy intervals,
     or "unknown" for unregistered / not-permitted
Times in the API are absolute instants (for example RFC 3339 with offset).
returns intervals, not event details, and only for invitees the caller is allowed to see.

All four behaviors work on a single database. Now harden the schema, write the query, and plan for growth past one node.

A relational database fits: the data is highly structured with clear relationships, and the marquee query is a set-based overlap. Store instants in UTC; keep the original zone and rule for correct display and recurrence expansion.

users(
  id            BIGINT PK,
  email         CITEXT UNIQUE,      -- case-insensitive, the invite lookup key
  password_hash TEXT,
  name          TEXT,
  home_timezone TEXT,               -- IANA zone, e.g. "America/New_York"
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ
)

calendars(
  id            BIGINT PK,
  owner_user_id BIGINT FK -> users(id),
  name          TEXT,
  default_visibility TEXT            -- free_busy | full | private
)

events(
  id            BIGINT PK,
  calendar_id   BIGINT FK -> calendars(id),
  organizer_user_id BIGINT FK -> users(id),
  title         TEXT,
  start_utc     TIMESTAMPTZ,        -- absolute instant
  end_utc       TIMESTAMPTZ,        -- half-open [start_utc, end_utc)
  start_timezone TEXT,              -- needed for DST-correct recurrence
  all_day       BOOLEAN,
  transparency  TEXT,               -- opaque = busy, transparent = free
  status        TEXT,               -- confirmed | cancelled
  recurrence_rule TEXT,             -- iCalendar RRULE, NULL if single
  recurrence_end_utc TIMESTAMPTZ,   -- bound for expansion
  updated_at    TIMESTAMPTZ
)

event_attendees(
  event_id      BIGINT FK -> events(id),
  user_id       BIGINT NULL FK -> users(id),  -- NULL = unregistered invitee
  invitee_email CITEXT,
  role          TEXT,               -- organizer | required | optional
  rsvp_status   TEXT,               -- needs_action | accepted | declined | tentative
  updated_at    TIMESTAMPTZ,
  PRIMARY KEY (event_id, invitee_email)
)

-- exceptions to a recurring series (a moved or cancelled instance)
event_overrides(
  parent_event_id  BIGINT FK -> events(id),
  occurrence_start_utc TIMESTAMPTZ,
  new_start_utc TIMESTAMPTZ NULL,
  new_end_utc   TIMESTAMPTZ NULL,
  cancelled     BOOLEAN,
  PRIMARY KEY (parent_event_id, occurrence_start_utc)
)

-- derived, read-optimized availability (recurrences pre-expanded)
busy_blocks(
  user_id       BIGINT,            -- shard key
  start_utc     TIMESTAMPTZ,
  end_utc       TIMESTAMPTZ,
  event_id      BIGINT,
  status        TEXT,              -- busy | tentative
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, start_utc, event_id)
)

Load an event with its attendees
Free/busy needs a per-user, time-ordered list of intervals with recurrences already expanded. Deriving that on the fly from
for many users is slow and, once sharded, cross-machine.
makes availability a local, index-friendly range scan — and it is exactly the table we fan out when sharding.
The query: is a group free during a time block?
. So a user is busy in the block
iff they have a busy interval satisfying that. The rest of the query is just filtering to "counts as busy".

-- Which of these users are BUSY in [:from, :to)?
SELECT DISTINCT user_id
FROM   busy_blocks
WHERE  user_id IN (:user_ids)
  AND  start_utc < :to
  AND  end_utc   > :from;
-- Users returned are busy; every requested user NOT returned is free.
Is the WHOLE group free? (a single boolean)

SELECT NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM   busy_blocks
  WHERE  user_id IN (:user_ids)
    AND  start_utc < :to
    AND  end_utc   > :from
) AS all_free;
From the normalized tables (no busy_blocks), single occurrences

SELECT DISTINCT ea.user_id
FROM   event_attendees ea
JOIN   events e ON e.id = ea.event_id
WHERE  ea.user_id IN (:user_ids)
  AND  ea.rsvp_status IN ('accepted','tentative')  -- declined is NOT busy
  AND  e.status       = 'confirmed'                -- cancelled is NOT busy
  AND  e.transparency = 'opaque'                   -- "free" events do not block
  AND  e.start_utc    < :to
  AND  e.end_utc      > :from;

To answer any range query — a calendar view or free/busy —
expand occurrences within the bounded window
, then apply overrides/exclusions. Two ways to make that cheap:
A user viewing their own day/week: expand that small window in the app.
Fine for narrow windows; not for free/busy across many users.
Availability: pre-expand each series across a rolling horizon (say the next 12 months) into per-user intervals.
Write amplification and a job to extend/repair the horizon; makes reads trivial and shardable.
for single events, but keep the

for recurring ones: “every weekday at 09:00 New York” maps to different UTC instants across a DST change. Expanding a recurrence by blindly adding 24 hours in UTC drifts by an hour twice a year — expand in the event's local zone, then convert each occurrence to UTC.

All-day events are date-based ("floating") and should be treated as busy for that local day, not a fixed UTC instant. DST transitions also create non-existent or doubled local times; pick and document a rule for those edge cases.

Partitioning past one database, and the issues

The central tension: an event spans many users
An event links an organizer and attendees who live on different shards. Where do the rows go, and how does per-user free/busy stay local?
A. Everything on the organizer's shard
Event + attendees stored once, with the organizer.
A user's own agenda is events organized by many other people, scattered across many shards. Free/busy for a set of invitees becomes a broad scatter/gather. Bad for the marquee read.
B. Fan out busy_blocks to each attendee's shard
Canonical event on the organizer's shard; on accept/change, upsert a derived
Write amplification and eventual consistency: an edit must reach every attendee shard.
Co-locate an event with its most-active participants.
Higher control-plane complexity; rarely worth it before B is exhausted.

free/busy and a user's agenda are the hot, latency-sensitive reads, and they become single-shard (or a bounded scatter across just the invited users' shards). The price is paid on the rarer write path.
How writes stay correct across shards

A relay publishes the outbox to a durable log —

A time change updates or replaces the affected blocks; a cancellation or decline removes them. Version each fan-out so a stale update cannot resurrect a deleted block.
A periodic job compares canonical events with derived blocks and repairs drift from lost messages.
just after an organizer moves a meeting, an invitee's free/busy can be seconds-stale. The organizer sees their own change immediately (same shard); others converge.
an all-hands with tens of thousands of invitees is a fan-out storm — batch it, and consider not materializing free/busy for very large or public events.
loading an event by id needs a map from event_id to the organizer's shard (embed the shard in the id, or keep a directory).
email→user_id is a global mapping, itself partitioned by email hash.
moving a user migrates both their calendar and their busy_blocks.

“I shard by user so per-user calendar and free/busy reads are local. An event's canonical row lives on the organizer's shard; I fan out derived busy blocks to each attendee's shard via a transactional outbox and idempotent workers. That trades write amplification and seconds of cross-user staleness for fast, single-shard availability reads, which is the hot path.”
Cache the read that users wait on
Short TTL; invalidate on any busy_blocks write for that user. A miss falls back to the shard.
Read replicas of the user's shard.
Replication lag of seconds is fine for others' data; read the primary for read-your-writes on your own edits.
Rarely changes; safe to cache with modest TTL.

Caching mostly saves work on popular scheduling queries and protects hot shards; it does not add durability. Because free/busy is already a cheap indexed range scan, the cache is an optimization, not the design's backbone. Keep invalidation tied to the same fan-out that writes
so the cache cannot mask a moved meeting for long.
route a user's own calendar reads to their primary (or a session-pinned replica) right after they write, so they never see their own edit disappear behind replication lag.
What happens when a component fails?
Stateless; the load balancer reroutes. Retries are safe if writes are idempotent.
In-flight requests retry; sessions live in a shared store, not the server.
Promote a replica; that user's writes pause briefly, reads continue from replicas.
Only users on that shard are affected; failover has a short window.
Serve others' data with labeled staleness; pin the user's own reads to the primary.
Free/busy of others may lag; never show your own edit as lost.
Outbox buffers; workers catch up; reconciliation repairs any gaps.
Cross-user free/busy is temporarily stale, not wrong forever.
Notifications stay queued and retry; event creation is unaffected.
Invite emails are delayed; in-app invites still appear.
Fall back to the shard/replica; slightly higher latency.
No correctness impact; capacity headroom needed for the miss storm.
Cache serves recent entries; new resolutions/onboarding may pause.
Do not guess a user's shard from stale data.
the canonical event and its many derived busy blocks
: a lost fan-out message silently makes someone look free when they are busy. Idempotent, versioned upserts plus reconciliation are what keep that honest.
One picture to explain the whole system

Blue = reads (calendar and free/busy), green = writes and busy-block fan-out, amber = async email. The schema sits inside the database box; the overlap query and the shard key are called out where they are used. The async fan-out is explicit:
Numbered boxes are discussion anchors. Redis / SES are illustrative choices, not requirements.

Browsers reach stateless app services through a load balancer. Calendar, invitation, and availability services read and write a relational database sharded by user_id, with read replicas and a free/busy cache. Event writes record a transactional outbox in the same transaction; a relay publishes it to Kafka, and a consumer group of fan-out workers upserts per-user busy_blocks onto each attendee's shard and pushes to an external email provider. The diagram labels the schema, the half-open overlap query, read and write paths, and the shard key.

Two trade-offs to say out loud
Fan-out busy_blocks: fast single-shard free/busy, at the cost of write amplification + seconds of cross-user staleness.
Recurrence + DST: expand in the event's local zone into busy_blocks; never range-query a bare RRULE.

Every box is a talking point: the API path, the services, the schema and its indexes, the overlap query, the async fan-out, and the shard key. Read modes and the consistency trade-off are labeled where they occur.

What you can say while you draw

“This is registration, events, email invitations, and free/busy for registered invitees. I will confirm recurrence, time zones, what free/busy exposes, and the consistency expectation, then sketch the architecture and the schema before details.”

“Browser to a load balancer and stateless app services — calendar, invitation, availability, auth — over a relational database with read replicas, a free/busy cache, and an async queue to an email provider.”
“Users, calendars, events with UTC instants plus zone and RRULE, event_attendees with RSVP, and a derived busy_blocks table keyed by user for availability. Intervals are half-open.”

“Free/busy is interval overlap: a user is busy if a block has start < the request end and end > the request start, filtering out declined, cancelled, and free events. Against busy_blocks it is a per-user index range scan; if the whole group must be free, wrap it in NOT EXISTS.”
5. Raise recurrence and time zones yourself
“A recurring series is one row but many occurrences, so I expand it — in the event's local zone for DST correctness — into busy_blocks over a rolling horizon. That keeps the query trivial.”

“Past one database I shard by user_id so a person's calendar and free/busy are local. The canonical event lives on the organizer's shard; I fan out busy_blocks to each attendee's shard via a transactional outbox published to Kafka and idempotent consumer workers. The trade-off is write amplification and seconds of cross-user staleness, which I mitigate with versioned upserts and reconciliation.”

“Reads are fast and mostly single-shard; writes do more work; free/busy of others is eventually consistent while your own calendar is read-your-writes. Caching and replicas are optimizations on top of an already-cheap query.”

for a single "all free" boolean. State the half-open intervals, the busy filter (exclude declined/cancelled/transparent), and that recurrence must be expanded first.
How would you partition, and what issues arise?

Covered in section 12. Shard by user_id; canonical event on the organizer's shard; fan out derived busy_blocks to attendee shards via an outbox → Kafka → idempotent consumer workers pipeline. Issues: eventual consistency of cross-user free/busy, fan-out hotspots for huge invite lists, an event_id→shard directory, a global email→user_id map, rebalancing, and unregistered invitees having no shard.
Why not store occurrences of recurring events as rows?

A rule can be unbounded ("every weekday forever"), so materializing all occurrences is impossible and editing the series would rewrite huge numbers of rows. Store the rule plus overrides, and expand within a bounded window (on read for a user's own view, or into busy_blocks over a rolling horizon for availability).
What advantages/disadvantages does your database choice have?

A relational engine fits structured data with foreign keys and the set-based overlap query, gives transactions for a consistent event + outbox write, and indexes range scans well. Disadvantages at scale: it does not shard itself, cross-shard joins are painful (hence denormalized busy_blocks), and very high write fan-out needs async workers. A document or wide-column store could scale writes but would push overlap logic and joins into the app; pick based on the access patterns, not familiarity.
How do you avoid double-booking or race conditions?

Free/busy is advisory, not a lock; two organizers can pick the same slot. If a hard "book a room/resource" is required, model the resource as an attendee with a uniqueness/constraint or a transaction that checks-and-inserts under the resource's row, so exactly one booking wins. Keep that scoped to resources rather than every user.

It returns intervals and status only, never titles or attendees, and only for invitees the caller is permitted to see (organizer of the event, or per the invitee's sharing setting). Unregistered emails return "unknown". Event details use a separate, more restrictive authorization path.
How would you support notifications/reminders at scale?

Reminders are scheduled notifications produced by a time-based worker reading upcoming events; sends are idempotent and deduplicated by (event, recipient, type). At scale, bucket reminders by fire-time and shard the workers; back-pressure via the queue.

The free/busy query: the exact mistakes to avoid
Across debriefs the overlap query is where answers break. The specific errors seen: testing only whether an event
the window (which misses a meeting that started earlier and is still running); storing a duration but never computing an

to compare against; leaving out the organizer's own events; writing SQL that would not actually run; and forgetting that a recurring series cannot be answered by a plain query. A strong answer, by contrast, joined events and attendees and filtered by time range and status correctly.

-- WRONG: only catches events that START inside the window, and has no
--        end boundary when just a duration was stored. Misses a 09:30-10:30
--        meeting for a 10:00-11:00 request; also omits the organizer.
SELECT ... WHERE start_utc >= :from AND start_utc < :to;

-- RIGHT: half-open interval overlap with a real end boundary, over rows
--        where recurrences are already expanded, including the organizer.
SELECT DISTINCT user_id
FROM   busy_blocks                          -- recurrences pre-expanded here
WHERE  user_id IN (:invitees_plus_organizer)
  AND  start_utc < :to                      -- starts before the window ends
  AND  end_utc   > :from;                   -- ...and ends after it starts
-- end_utc is stored or derived as start_utc + duration, and indexed.
Two half-open intervals overlap iff each starts before the other ends — that single predicate is the whole trick. Keep
